authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — unreviewed candidate generation

items.prompt: The task is the shortest contiguous range with sum at least T, and values may be negative. Which observation is the strongest signal that the simple positive-value window is unsafe?
constraints: The proposed algorithm stops shrinking when the current sum falls below T.
No additional monotonic data structure is maintained.

options.text: Removing a negative left value can raise the sum, so an invalid window can become valid after further shrinking.
The candidate is contiguous.
The answer is a minimum length.
The inputs are integers.

feedback.reason: The attempted stopping rule requires further shrinking to preserve invalidity; a negative outgoing value can reverse that assumption.

blocks.text: The positive-value algorithm relies on a monotone boundary: after a left removal makes `sum < T`, later removals cannot restore `sum >= T`. Signed values invalidate that implication because removing a negative contribution increases the sum. Contiguity and a shortest objective do not establish a legal discard rule, so the method must preserve multiple competing starts instead of committing to one `left`.

blocks.title: What the general signed method preserves
blocks.text: A standard general solution uses prefix sums and a monotonic deque. The deque stores candidate start boundaries in increasing prefix-sum order, removes older tail candidates dominated by a later no-larger prefix, and removes front candidates once their difference from the current prefix reaches T. This supplies a different proof from a simple one-left-boundary window.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_is_contiguous: Contiguity identifies the candidate shape but not whether a one-way shrink rule can safely discard starts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.answer_is_shortest: Many shortest-range objectives lack monotonicity; the objective name does not validate the strategy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_are_integers: Integer type permits negative contributions and supplies no directional guarantee.

items.prompt: Consider the rule ‘if sum > 3, shrink left until sum ≤ 3; record when sum = 3’ on [4, -2, 1]. Which trace proves the rule can miss a valid range?
constraints: The whole range [4, -2, 1] sums to 3.
The algorithm processes values left to right and never moves left backward.

options.text: The target 3 is not an integer representable by the algorithm.
At the first value, sum = 4 causes 4 to be discarded; the later −2 and 1 would have brought that same start back to the exact target.
The whole range is not contiguous because it contains a negative value.
The rule fails only because the required length was not provided.

feedback.reason: With signed values, a start that is currently over target can become exactly valid after later expansion, so shrinking discards it without proof.

blocks.text: After reading 4, the proposed comparison-based rule assumes that keeping this start can never help and removes it. That assumption is valid for positive exact/threshold behaviour only under carefully stated objectives. Here the next contributions are −2 and +1, so the untouched prefix would evolve from 4 to 2 to 3 and form a qualifying range. Because left never moves backward, the algorithm cannot recover it. Prefix-difference state retains all prior starts instead of making this unsupported discard.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_not_integer: The target is an ordinary integer; representation is unrelated to the lost start boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_not_contiguous: Signs do not affect contiguity. The three adjacent positions form one contiguous range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.needs_fixed_length: Exact-sum ranges can have variable lengths; the failure comes from a non-monotone sum, not missing k.

items.prompt: After one preprocessing pass, a system must answer many arbitrary range-sum queries [l, r] presented in any order. Which fact is the decisive signal against using one moving sliding window as the primary query mechanism?
constraints: Every query still refers to a contiguous range.
Successive query endpoints may jump left or right with no monotone order.

options.text: Every query is contiguous, so one sliding window is automatically optimal.
Sort the array values before answering so every requested range becomes easy to slide.
A single window would need to move boundaries backward or rebuild state for arbitrary query order; prefix sums answer each range from two stored prefixes.
Use a fixed-size window whose length equals the number of queries.

feedback.reason: A sliding window gains efficiency from one monotone sweep; arbitrary query endpoints destroy that traversal order, while prefix sums retain reusable range state.

blocks.text: Each query names a contiguous interval, but contiguity is not the only requirement for a moving window. A window reuses state when the next candidate is adjacent to the previous one and its boundaries continue forward. Arbitrary queries can jump from [100..200] to [3..8] and then to [70..900], forcing backward moves or reconstruction. Prefix sums preprocess cumulative state once and answer every [l..r] as prefix[r+1] − prefix[l] regardless of query order. An offline algorithm may reorder queries under a separate contract, but that is not the simple single-sweep window assumed here.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.contiguous_means_window: Contiguity defines each candidate, but arbitrary ordering prevents the one-out/one-in monotone reuse that gives a sliding window its advantage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_queries: Sorting the input values changes the elements inside each original index range and therefore changes every requested answer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_query_count: The number of queries has no relation to any query interval's length or to the state required for its sum.

items.prompt: A range is valid only when its median equals M. Without an additional data structure or proof, why is ‘expand, then shrink until valid’ not a justified simple window rule?
constraints: Values are arbitrary.
The median is the middle ordered value, using the task's fixed convention when the range length is even.
The rule has no monotone predicate beyond median == M.

options.text: Numeric statistics are never compatible with windows.
A window may use only ≤ or ≥ predicates, never equality.
Sorting the whole input preserves every original contiguous range and fixes the issue.
Adding or removing one value can move the median above, below, or back to M, so no single directional repair/discard rule is established.

feedback.reason: A simple variable window needs a proof that one boundary move restores validity and safely discards excluded starts; median equality supplies no such monotonicity by itself.

blocks.text: The median is the middle value after ordering the values currently inside the range, under the declared even-length convention. Window feasibility is not determined by whether a statistic is numeric or uses equality; it needs directional control. With arbitrary values, adding one element can move the median in either direction, and removing the leftmost element can do the same. A currently invalid range therefore does not identify a safe discard. Specialized data structures can maintain the median efficiently, but they do not automatically prove a one-way shrink policy. Sorting the whole input destroys original contiguity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.median_is_numeric: Sums, counts, and many numeric aggregates are window-compatible when their validity behaviour is proven.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.equality_is_forbidden: Some exact conditions are window-compatible under stronger constraints; the missing property is a safe boundary rule, not the equality symbol itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.needs_sorting_once: Global sorting changes which elements are adjacent and therefore changes the legal ranges.

items.prompt: A longest-window implementation shrinks while `currentLength <= bestLength` and stops when the answer would change. What is the decisive defect?
constraints: The problem also has an explicit validity constraint.
bestLength is historical global state, not the current window predicate.

options.text: Shrinking must be controlled by current validity; comparing with the historical answer neither restores the invariant nor proves a start can be discarded.
The only defect is that bestLength should decrease during shrinking.
Window length must never appear in a sliding-window solution.
The loop should always be replaced with exactly one left move.

feedback.reason: Boundary movement is justified by the current window invariant, not by whether the global answer changes.

blocks.text: The global best summarizes earlier legal candidates. It does not say whether the current range violates its budget, frequency cap, or other predicate. Shrinking a valid range merely because it is not longer can discard starts needed for future expansions; failing to shrink an invalid range because its length is promising leaves state illegal. The loop condition must name the violation being repaired, and the answer update occurs at the legal state prescribed by the objective. The answer is an output accumulator, not a control invariant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.best_should_decrease: A maximum accumulator should not decrease; the error is using it to control boundary legality.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.length_never_matters: Length is often the answer, but it cannot substitute for a separate validity predicate unless length itself is the fixed constraint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shrink_once_only: A variable violation may need zero, one, or many removals; the correct count follows the invariant.

items.prompt: A fixed-size task asks for the maximum sum of exactly k consecutive values, and values may be negative. Does negativity invalidate the fixed-size sliding window?
constraints: k is a positive integer.
Every candidate has exactly k elements.
The running sum removes one outgoing value and adds one incoming value.

options.text: Yes. Any negative value makes every sliding window invalid.
No. The update is exact algebraic replacement, not a monotone shrink decision, so signs do not affect correctness.
It remains valid only if values are sorted.
Replace each value by its absolute value before sliding.

feedback.reason: Negative values break some monotone variable-window rules, not the exact one-out/one-in maintenance of a fixed-size aggregate.

blocks.text: The fixed-size invariant is purely representational: the sum equals the values between boundaries and the range contains exactly k elements. Moving the window right subtracts the value that leaves and adds the value that enters, which is correct for any signed numbers. No decision assumes that expansion raises the sum or shrinking lowers it. Therefore ‘negative values’ is a targeted failure signal for certain sum-threshold windows, not a universal ban on sliding windows.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_negative_break: Signs do not affect exact subtraction/addition for a predetermined range size.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_sorted: Original order defines contiguity; sorting is unnecessary and would change the candidate ranges.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.convert_absolute: Absolute values change every candidate sum and solve a different problem.

items.prompt: A variable window increments left while shrinking but does not remove the outgoing value from its frequency map. What failure signal is present?

options.text: The maintained state no longer represents the current [left,right] range, so the validity test is about a different window.
The method is unsafe only when input values can be negative.
The bug is harmless because every window has two boundaries.
The frequency map should be replaced with sorting after every shrink.

feedback.reason: A window invariant includes synchronized boundaries and state updates for entering and leaving values.

blocks.text: When left advances, the old left value exits and its count must decrease or be deleted. Otherwise the algorithm may believe the range is still invalid after the responsible value has left, or may report a constraint violation for a value no longer present. The issue applies regardless of sign.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_values_only: Frequency-state synchronization is a correctness requirement even for strings or nonnegative values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_window_safe: Two boundaries do not automatically keep aggregate state aligned.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_needed: Sorting is unrelated to removing an outgoing frequency contribution.

items.prompt: A shortest-valid-window implementation records the current length immediately after expanding right, before shrinking an invalid range. What answer defect can follow?

options.text: It can record a range that violates the predicate, so the answer is not guaranteed to be valid.
It can affect only longest-window tasks, never shortest-window tasks.
It merely records the same valid range twice without changing correctness.
It is wrong only when values are negative.

feedback.reason: An answer update must respect the problem's validity predicate and the objective's timing boundary.

blocks.text: For a shortest valid range, expand, repair until valid, then record the repaired candidate—often recording each valid shrink for the shortest objective. Scoring before repair can accept excess distinct values, an over-budget sum, or another invalid state. Sign assumptions do not excuse recording a violated predicate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.miss_longest_only: Shortest objectives are equally sensitive to recording invalid ranges.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_state: The recorded range may contain the violation, not merely duplicate a valid answer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_sum: The order is wrong even when the validity predicate is monotone.

items.prompt: The proposed solution removes arbitrary old elements from a collection until a constraint holds, but the output must be a contiguous subarray. What structural signal invalidates it?

options.text: Arbitrary removals no longer represent one [left,right] interval, so the maintained candidate can violate the output shape.
The solution uses too many indices; a window may use only one pointer.
Any auxiliary collection is forbidden in a window.
Every contiguous problem must have a fixed window length.

feedback.reason: A sliding window represents a contiguous interval, so its outgoing elements must be exactly the prefix left of the current boundary.

blocks.text: Removing arbitrary members creates a subsequence or set rather than a contiguous range. A valid window may maintain maps, counters, deques, or other state, and it may be fixed or variable size; the invariant is interval membership, not the number of pointers.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.too_many_indices: Two boundaries are normal for a window and are not the defect.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_forbidden: Auxiliary state is often essential to maintain validity incrementally.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_size_required: Variable-size windows are valid when their shrink predicate is justified.

items.prompt: Select all review signals that should block blindly applying a positive-value shortest-threshold window rule.

options.text: Values may be negative, so removing the left value can increase the sum or future additions can rescue an earlier start.
The validity predicate can become true, false, and true again as left advances with no proven monotonic repair.
The task is fixed-size and only asks for an aggregate of each exact-length block.
The code uses variables named left and right.

feedback.reason: The variable positive-threshold rule needs a monotone sum and a proof that discarded starts cannot become useful again.

blocks.text: Negative contributions and nonmonotone predicates remove the directional guarantee behind shrinkage. Fixed-size windows use a different, exact-length invariant and are not automatically blocked by negative values. Variable names supply no proof.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_size: Fixed-size maintenance can remain valid with negative values because it adds one value and removes the value k positions old.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_direction_names: Names do not determine the effect of boundary movement.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.negative_values: Signed values can invalidate both monotone repair and discarded-start dominance.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.nonmonotone_predicate: Without a restoration theorem, repeated shrinkage is only a loop shape, not a safe algorithm.

items.prompt: Why can a variable-size sum window fail on arrays containing negative values even when the code shrinks while sum exceeds a target?
constraints: The array may contain positive and negative values.
The objective relies on monotonicity of the window sum.

options.text: Adding an item can decrease the sum and removing one can increase it, so the usual expand-then-shrink proof no longer holds.
options.explanation: Positive-number monotonicity is the missing precondition.

options.text: The code is correct; it only needs a faster left pointer.
options.explanation: Speed does not restore a false monotonicity premise.

options.text: Negative values always imply the window must have fixed length.
options.explanation: Other methods such as prefix sums may solve variable ranges.

options.text: The sum predicate is irrelevant because windows are defined only by frequencies.
options.explanation: The stated predicate is numeric and depends on values.

feedback.reason: The classic threshold shrink rule depends on positive contributions making sum monotone under expansion and shrink.

blocks.text: With signed values, a currently oversized window may become valid after expansion, and removing the leftmost value may increase the sum. A different state method or stronger predicate is required.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shrink_too_slow: Speed does not restore a false monotonicity premise.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_size_needed: Other methods such as prefix sums may solve variable ranges.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.frequency_only: The stated predicate is numeric and depends on values.

items.prompt: Which signal indicates that a two-pointer window is solving the wrong problem because the required elements need not be contiguous?
constraints: The output may select arbitrary indices.
Contiguity is not part of the objective.

options.text: The task is a subset or pair selection problem over the whole input, so a contiguous window cannot represent all legal solutions.
options.explanation: A window encodes one interval of indices.

options.text: Keep the window model and move both pointers faster to reach noncontiguous combinations.
options.explanation: Pointer speed cannot represent a set with gaps.

options.text: Sort the input first so every arbitrary subset becomes contiguous.
options.explanation: Sorting changes index relationships and still does not encode arbitrary choices.

options.text: Use the full array as one window because it contains every legal subset.
options.explanation: Containing items is not equivalent to selecting a subset under the output contract.

feedback.reason: A window is a contiguous index interval; it cannot express arbitrary selections with gaps.

blocks.text: The first diagnostic is to translate the output contract into index geometry. If legal answers are noncontiguous, use a method whose state can represent chosen positions rather than adding pointer heuristics.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.move_faster: Pointer speed cannot represent a set with gaps.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_input: Sorting changes index relationships and still does not encode arbitrary choices.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.longer_window: Containing items is not equivalent to selecting a subset under the output contract.

items.prompt: A window predicate depends on insertion order but the algorithm treats it as a set property and repairs only counts. What defect is likely?
constraints: The predicate is sensitive to relative order or positions.
The state stores only aggregate frequencies.

options.text: The window state omits an order-sensitive fact, so equal counts can represent different validity outcomes.
options.explanation: The summary is not sufficient for the predicate.

options.text: Counts are always sufficient because every window predicate is permutation-invariant.
Move the left pointer without adding any order state; the missing information will emerge automatically.
options.explanation: Pointer movement cannot recover discarded order information.

options.text: Sort each window to make the aggregate counts reliable.
options.explanation: Sorting changes the original order that the predicate observes.

feedback.reason: A sliding-window invariant is valid only when its stored summary is sufficient for the actual predicate.

blocks.text: Frequency maps capture permutation-invariant constraints such as distinct-count limits. If validity depends on order, adjacency, or last occurrence, those facts must be represented explicitly.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.left_boundary_only: Pointer movement cannot recover discarded order information.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_window: Sorting changes the original order that the predicate observes.

items.prompt: Why is resetting the left pointer to zero after every invalid expansion a warning sign in a linear sliding-window algorithm?
constraints: The input is scanned left to right.
The intended complexity is amortized linear.

options.text: Resetting can revisit a long prefix many times, so the pointer no longer moves monotonically and total work can become quadratic.
options.explanation: Linear amortization requires each boundary to advance only forward.

options.text: Resetting is required because every window must begin at index zero.
options.explanation: Valid windows can begin at later indices.

options.text: Resetting converts any variable window into a correct fixed-size scan.
options.explanation: It changes neither the predicate nor the output contract correctly.

options.text: Resetting primarily increases memory rather than runtime.
options.explanation: The main defect is repeated work, not stored state.

feedback.reason: The linear sliding-window proof charges each pointer movement once; resets invalidate that amortization.

blocks.text: A reset can reprocess the same elements after each violation. Unless the problem has a separate proven restart structure, the left boundary should advance monotonically and preserve the invariant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_required: Valid windows can begin at later indices.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_window: It changes neither the predicate nor the output contract correctly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memory_leak: The main defect is repeated work, not stored state.
